idea: Rotating right by k moves the last k elements to the front. The trick for doing it in place: reversing the whole array, then each part, puts every element in its rotated spot.
analogy: Shuffling a deck by cutting it: take the bottom k cards and put them on top. Reversing the deck and then each pile does the same cut without a second table.

computeWithExtraArray.summary: Copy each element straight to its new index (i + k) % n.
steps: k = k % n, so rotating by n or more doesn't repeat work.
Write nums[i] into result[(i + k) % n].
Copy the result back into nums.
computeWithExtraArray.timeWhy: One pass plus the copy back.

computeWithReverse.summary: Reverse all, then reverse the first k, then the rest.
computeWithReverse.timeWhy: Each element is swapped about twice.

computeWithArrayList.summary: Move the last element to the front, k times.
steps: k times: remove the last element and insert it at index 0.
computeWithArrayList.timeWhy: Inserting at the front shifts every element, k times.

computeWithCyclic.summary: Each element jumps straight to its final place, displacing the next one along the cycle.
steps: From start, carry the value to (current + k) % n, pick up what was there, and keep going.
When you return to start, the cycle is done; move start forward.
count stops the loop once all n elements have moved (needed when n and k share a factor).

pitfalls: Forgetting k = k % n (k can be larger than n).
An empty array makes k % n throw ArithmeticException (division by zero).
Rotate right versus left changes which part you reverse.
interview: Show the reversal trick on the 7-element example; it's easier to justify than cyclic replacement.
Say the in-place requirement out loud: it's why the extra array isn't the final answer.
